Learning happens through small corrections (governed by learning rate α) to Q-values each time the agent sees a mismatch between what it expected and what it observed. Convergence requires repeated episodes because early Q-estimates are based on incomplete information; only after many tries does the agent discover better paths and update its estimates closer to reality.

Why One Episode Is Not Enough
After just one run, Q-values are still wrong or unstable because the agent has not yet discovered all important information.
The robot may not have discovered the path to the goal yet.
It may not have experienced the large positive reward (+10) at the goal.
Early Q-estimates are based on only the small, local rewards seen so far (e.g., −1, −2, −1).
These estimates do not yet reflect the true long-term value of actions.
A Q-value learned from a single episode without ever seeing the goal is not the true value — it is an incomplete estimate. Do not rely on single-episode learning to converge.
Q-values converge to their true values only after many repeated episodes in which the agent explores different paths, discovers better routes, and refines its estimates.
Robot tries one path, updates Q-values based on rewards seen along that path.
Robot takes different actions (exploration), discovers new states and rewards, updates Q-values again.
Over time, the robot discovers better paths, including routes to the goal, and sees the large reward. These discoveries propagate backward through Q-value updates.
After many episodes, Q-values stabilize — they stop changing significantly. This signals that the robot has learned the optimal policy.

Reinforcement Learning Foundations

Reinforcement Learning Foundations
Overview
What: Establishing what RL is, why it differs from supervised and unsupervised learning, and when to use it.
How it breaks down:
Three Branches of Machine Learning — where RL sits relative to supervised and unsupervised approaches
Core Components and the "No Teacher" Principle — the five moving parts of an RL system and why learning without explicit instruction is the defining feature
Applications and the Exploration-Exploitation Dilemma — when to use RL and the central tension it must resolve
Takeaway: RL is chosen precisely when you have sequential feedback but no fixed answer key — the environment itself is the teacher, and the agent must balance trying new things against exploiting what it already knows works.
Three Branches of Machine Learning
Supervised Learning
Supervised Learning: Maps input to output using labeled training examples (answer key provided).
Analogy: A student with an answer key — the correct output is always available for comparison.
Unsupervised Learning
Unsupervised Learning: Discovers hidden patterns in unlabeled data without output guidance.
Analogy: An explorer finding tribes — no map provided, patterns emerge from the structure of the data itself.
Reinforcement Learning
Reinforcement Learning: Learning which action to take based on rewards and punishments received from the environment.
Analogy: A pet learning tricks for treats — feedback is sequential, immediate, and tied to specific actions rather than a fixed dataset.
Core Components and the "No Teacher" Principle
The Five Core Components
Agent: The learner (e.g., a robot).
Environment: The world the agent interacts with (e.g., a grid or game board).
Action: What the agent can do (e.g., move up, down, left, right).
State: Where the agent is or what it observes (e.g., a specific cell in the grid).
Reward: Feedback signal indicating quality of an outcome (positive for good, negative for bad, zero for neutral).
The "No Teacher" Principle
No Teacher Principle: The agent receives no instructions or map — only reward feedback. It must learn which actions lead to better outcomes by accumulation.
Scenario: Agent explores an unknown environment with only feedback signals (warmer/colder as small rewards, goal/penalty as large rewards).
Learning process: Agent takes actions, receives rewards or penalties, and gradually improves by recognizing which actions lead to better total outcomes.
Core insight: No correct path is given upfront; the agent discovers it through trial and feedback.
This absence of an explicit teacher is what fundamentally separates RL from supervised learning and is the reason RL requires a different algorithmic approach.
Applications and When to Use RL
When RL Is the Right Choice

Use RL when you have a clear reward signal but no dataset of correct (input, output) pairs and when the environment is dynamic or partially unknown.
The Exploration-Exploitation Dilemma
Exploration-Exploitation Dilemma: The tension between doing what is already known to work (exploit) versus trying something new that might be better (explore).
Exploitation: Greedy choice — selecting the action with the highest known Q-value (reward estimate).
Exploration: Random choice — trying a new action to discover better paths or rewards.
Pure exploitation leads to getting stuck in local optima; pure exploration wastes time on suboptimal actions. The right balance is central to RL success.
Value Functions and Q-Learning
Overview
What: Introducing the concept of value functions as the memory system for learning, and Q-Learning as the algorithm that estimates and updates them.
How it breaks down:
Value Functions: State and State-Action — two ways to rate how good a situation is
Q-Learning Algorithm Basics — the framework and Q-value table structure
The Bellman Equation — the recursive principle that connects observed and expected Q-values
Takeaway: A Q-value is a learned estimate of the total future reward from taking a specific action in a specific state. Q-Learning stores and updates these estimates in a table; the Bellman equation is the rule that ties each Q-value to the rewards and future possibilities it represents.
Value Functions: State and State-Action
State Value Function V(s)
State Value V(s): A scalar that rates how good it is to be in state s, independent of any specific action.
Represents the long-term total reward expected from that state onward.
Input: a state s; Output: a number indicating value.
State-Action Value Function Q(s,a)
State-Action Value Q(s,a): A scalar that rates how good it is to take action a in state s.
Represents the long-term total reward expected after taking that specific action from that state.
Input: a state s and an action a; Output: a number indicating quality of that action in that state.
More informative than V(s) because it guides which action to take.
Q-Learning estimates and updates Q(s,a) values. The goal is to learn Q-values that maximize the total cumulative reward the agent receives.
Q-Value Table Structure
Q-Value Table: A matrix where rows are states, columns are actions, and each cell stores Q(s,a) for that state-action pair.

At the start of learning, Q-values can be initialized arbitrarily (often 0 or random). The algorithm corrects them over time through experience.
Q-Learning Algorithm Basics
Value-Based Methods
Value-Based Method: An RL approach that learns a value function, which is then used to determine the optimal policy (which action to take in each state).
The value function (Q-values) is the primary learning target.
The policy is derived by selecting actions that maximize the value function.
Q-Learning as a Value-Based Algorithm
Q-Learning: A value-based RL algorithm that learns Q(s,a) values through iterative updates based on observed rewards and transitions.
Agent starts in a state (e.g., S₁).
Agent takes an action according to an exploration policy (e.g., random choice, not based on Q-values).
Agent transitions to a new state and receives a reward.
Q-value is updated using the Bellman equation and a learning rule.
Process repeats until the episode ends (goal reached or failure) or across many episodes until convergence.
Q-Learning is off-policy: it learns the optimal policy while following an exploratory behavior policy. This means it can learn the best strategy even while taking random or suboptimal actions.
The Bellman Equation
Bellman Equation for Q-Values
Bellman Equation: A recursive principle stating that the Q-value of taking action a in state s equals the immediate reward plus the discounted maximum future Q-value from the next state.
Observed Q-value (Bellman Equation)

Q(s,a)_observed: The true or observed value estimate of taking action a in state s.
R(s'): The immediate reward received upon arriving in the next state s'.
γ (gamma): The discount factor — a value between 0 and 1 that determines how much the agent values future rewards relative to immediate rewards.
max_a' Q(s', a'): The maximum Q-value available in the next state (the best action to take there).
The Bellman equation is the foundation of Q-Learning. You must be able to identify its components and compute Q(s,a)_observed from a given reward and next-state Q-values.
Discount Factor γ (Gamma)
Discount Factor γ: A parameter between 0 and 1 that controls how much the agent values future rewards compared to immediate rewards.

A higher γ makes the robot more tolerant of short-term negative rewards when long-term future rewards are promising. Choose γ based on the problem: distant goals need higher γ.
Q-Learning Updates and Convergence
Overview
What: The mechanics of how Q-values are updated step by step, and why multiple episodes are essential for learning convergence.
How it breaks down:
Temporal Difference Error and the Update Rule — how the difference between observed and expected Q-values drives learning
Worked Examples: Step-by-Step Updates — three concrete grid transitions showing the update process
Episodes and Convergence — why one attempt is not enough and how repeated episodes lead to a stable, optimal policy
Takeaway: Learning happens through small corrections (governed by learning rate α) to Q-values each time the agent sees a mismatch between what it expected and what it observed. Convergence requires repeated episodes because early Q-estimates are based on incomplete information; only after many tries does the agent discover better paths and update its estimates closer to reality.
Temporal Difference Error and the Update Rule
Temporal Difference Error (TDE)
Temporal Difference Error: The difference between the observed Q-value (from the Bellman equation) and the current expected Q-value stored in the table.
Temporal Difference Error

Q(s,a)_observed: What the Bellman equation says the Q-value should be, based on this transition.
Q(s,a)_expected: What we currently have stored in the Q-table.
TDE: Positive if the observed value is higher (pleasant surprise); negative if lower (disappointing discovery).
TDE is the "learning signal" — it tells the algorithm how wrong its current Q-estimate is. A TDE of 0 means the Q-value is correct; non-zero TDE triggers an update.
Q-Value Update Rule
Update Rule: The mechanism for adjusting a Q-value based on the temporal difference error and a learning rate.
Q-Value Update

Q(s,a)_new: The updated Q-value to store in the table.
α (alpha): The learning rate (step size) — controls how much of the error signal we act on in one update.
TDE: The temporal difference error computed above.
You must be able to compute the update rule given α, a TDE, and the old Q-value. The result replaces the old value in the table.
Learning Rate α (Alpha)
Learning Rate α: A parameter between 0 and 1 that scales how much of the temporal difference error is incorporated into each update.
Small α (e.g., 0.1): Conservative updates; the agent slowly corrects its Q-values. Useful when there is noise in rewards.
Large α (e.g., 0.9): Aggressive updates; the agent quickly adopts new information. Risk of instability if rewards are noisy.
α = 1: The new Q-value is entirely the observed value; the old estimate is discarded.
In practice, α is often reduced over time (schedule) to stabilize convergence: large updates early to explore, smaller updates later to refine.

Episodes and Convergence
What Is an Episode?
Episode: One complete run of the agent from start (or random initial state) to goal (or failure).
Episode starts: Agent placed in a starting state (e.g., S₁, or randomly chosen).
Episode ends: Agent reaches the goal state (e.g., S₉ with +10 reward) or a terminal failure state (e.g., S₈ with −10 penalty).
Example episode: S₁ →(down)→ S₄ →(right)→ S₅ →(right)→ S₆ ... (continues until reaching S₈ or S₉).
Why One Episode Is Not Enough
Single Episode Problem: After just one run, Q-values are still wrong or unstable because the agent has not yet discovered all important information.
The robot may not have discovered the path to the goal yet.
It may not have experienced the large positive reward (+10) at the goal.
Early Q-estimates are based on only the small, local rewards seen so far (e.g., −1, −2, −1).
These estimates do not yet reflect the true long-term value of actions.
A Q-value learned from a single episode without ever seeing the goal is not the true value — it is an incomplete estimate. Do not rely on single-episode learning to converge.
Why Multiple Episodes Are Needed
Convergence Principle: Q-values converge to their true values only after many repeated episodes in which the agent explores different paths, discovers better routes, and refines its estimates.
Episode 1: Robot tries one path, updates Q-values based on rewards seen along that path.
Episode 2: Robot takes different actions (exploration), discovers new states and rewards, updates Q-values again.
Episode 3+: Over time, the robot discovers better paths, including routes to the goal, and sees the large reward. These discoveries propagate backward through Q-value updates.
Convergence: After many episodes, Q-values stabilize — they stop changing significantly. This signals that the robot has learned the optimal policy.
The Learning Process: Each episode provides more experience and corrects Q-values closer to their true values. The key insight is that discovering high rewards (like +10 at the goal) retroactively improves the Q-estimates of states that lead there, even if those states were visited in earlier episodes.
Convergence to Optimal Policy
Convergence: The point at which Q-values stop changing significantly across episodes, indicating the agent has learned a stable, near-optimal policy.
When convergence is reached: From any state, the agent knows which action has the highest Q-value — this is the optimal greedy action.
How to recognize it: Track the maximum absolute change in any Q-value per episode. When this change becomes very small (e.g., < 0.01), learning is effectively done.
/
After convergence: The agent can switch from exploration to pure exploitation — always taking the action with the highest Q-value — and will achieve near-optimal total reward.
The exam will test your understanding of why multiple episodes are necessary: single-episode learning is incomplete because the agent has not yet discovered all reward-bearing paths and their true long-term values. Convergence requires repeated exploration and learning.
